query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Laser peening induces compressive residual stress, which enhances the resistance to corrosion of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications by refining grain size and increasing dislocation density.
generation.material_initial_state: 304L stainless steel with a thickness of 25 mm
generation.intervention: Laser peening with an Nd-YAG laser, 4.4 J energy, and a water layer of 1~2 mm
generation.conditions: Room temperature, 1% NaCl solution at 30 °C, and deaerated at a rate of 200 mL N2/min for 30 min
generation.structural_mediator: Compressive residual stress, grain refinement, and increased dislocation density
generation.mechanism: The compressive residual stress induced by laser peening reduces the tendency for crack propagation and increases the energy required for corrosion to occur, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved corrosion resistance, reduced intergranular corrosion rate, and increased polarization resistance
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold for steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, with similar composition and microstructure to 304L stainless steel, and subjected to similar laser peening conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The effect of laser peening on corrosion resistance may be influenced by factors such as surface roughness, absorption layer quality, and static load, which are not fully understood and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the corrosion resistance of laser-peened and untreated 304L stainless steel specimens in a controlled environment, using techniques such as intergranular corrosion rate measurement, anodic polarization test, and AC impedance test.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-peened specimens exhibit significantly lower corrosion resistance than the untreated specimens, the hypothesis is falsified.

When laser peening is performed, plasma is concentrated on the surface using a transparent overlay (water [] or glass [] layer), and absorption layers (Al [,], vinyl tape [,]) are used to form effective compressive residual stress. When laser peening is performed by positioning an absorption layer that maintains the high quality of the surface and effectively maintains surface melting and energy conversion, compressive residual stress is formed [] and grain refinement occurs [], which leads to microstructural changes due to increasing dislocation density and strain []. This influences intergranular corrosion, corrosion fatigue, and SCC properties. We recently reported the effect of laser peening on the microstructure of 304L stainless steel: Laser peening resulted in the increased roughness of the surface, refinement of the grain size, deformation of the inside, increased dislocation density, and increased hardness of 304L stainless steel [].

In this study, we made laser-peened 304L stainless steel, which has a compressive residual stress of over 1 mm, evaluated intergranular corrosion properties and polarization behavior, and measured residual stress. Resistances were discussed and the effect of laser peening on corrosion properties was elucidated.
## 2.1. Specimen
The specimen used in this work was commercial 304L stainless steel; Table 1 shows the chemical composition of 304L stainless steel and its filler metal []. The thickness of the specimen was 25 mm. ## 2.2. Laser Peening (LP)
The laser peening process employed in this study was well described elsewhere: Figure 1 shows the schematic diagram of laser peening and Table 4 summarizes the laser peening conditions []. The test solution was 0.5 M H2SO4 + 0.01 M KSCN at 30 °C and was deaerated at a rate of 200 mL N2/min for 30 min. A DL-EPR test was performed using a potentiostat (Interface 1000, Gamry Instruments, Warminster, PA, USA). Pt wire and a saturated calomel electrode were used as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. Anodic scan to vertex potential (+400 mV(SCE)) and reactivation were swept, and the scan rate was at a rate of 1.677 mV/s. According to the standard [], the ratio of Ir/Ia was determined, indicating the degree of sensitization (DOS).
After the test, the specimen was taken out and ultrasonically cleaned, and the cross-section was observed using an optical microscope (AXIOTECH 100 HD, ZEISS, Oberkochen, Germany).

## 2.7. AC Impedance Test
The specimens were cut to sizes of 15 × 15 × 10 mm. The specimen and potentiostat used were the same as with the anodic polarization test. The test solution was 1% NaCl at 30 °C and deaerated at a rate of 200 mL N2/min for 30 min. The frequency range was 0.01~10,000 Hz, and an AC impedance test was performed at the corrosion potential. Polarization resistance was calculated using an equivalent circuit of Randles model [].
## 2.8. Residual Stress Measurement
The residual stress was performed via a hole drilling method (RS-200 Assembly, VMM, USA). A strain gauge was attached and holes were fabricated by using a drilling device. The residual stresses released during the drilling were measured.
